Grid-Hardening Opportunity Map

Which U.S. electric utilities face the most pole-breaking storms and wildfire risk, measured against their storm outage history and size? Built entirely from public federal data.

Utility territories are approximated by the counties each utility reports serving to EIA. A county listed means the utility serves some customers there, not all. See methods.

Click a utility in the table to outline its counties and see the numbers behind its score. Click a county on the map to see which utilities serve it.

Score weights

Each input is converted to a percentile (0–100) among the ranked utilities. The score is the weighted average. Drag to change what matters most; the table and map update instantly.

Methods, in plain English

The question: which utilities would benefit most from stronger, fire-resistant poles? This page measures need only: exposure to pole-breaking weather and wildfire, how much major storms already cost customers in outage time, and how many customers a utility serves. It makes no claims about any pole product's performance or cost.

The four inputs

InputWhat it measuresSource
Storm exposureHow often pole-breaking storms hit the counties a utility serves: thunderstorm wind, high wind, hurricane, tropical storm, ice storm, tornado and wildfire reports, per 1,000 square miles per year, 2016–2025. Dividing by area keeps big Western counties from looking stormy just because they're big.NOAA Storm Events Database
WildfireThe average of two national percentiles for each county: wildfire likelihood, and risk to homes (likelihood × how much damage a fire would do). Counties are weighted by how many buildings they have, because poles go where customers are.USDA Forest Service, Wildfire Risk to Communities
Storm outage minutesOutage minutes per customer on "major event days" (the big-storm days), averaged over 2021–2025: total SAIDI minus SAIDI without major event days. Averaging five years keeps one bad storm year from dominating. Uses the IEEE 1366 method only, so every utility's storm days are defined the same way; at least 3 of 5 years are required.EIA Form 861, Reliability
CustomersRetail customers on the utility's own wires in 2025, ranked on a log scale so a 60,000-customer co-op and a 6-million-customer utility both register.EIA Form 861, Sales and Delivery Companies

Each input becomes a percentile among ranked utilities, so different units share one 0–100 scale. The score is the weighted average of the four percentiles (equal weights by default). The formula above updates as you move the sliders.

Gaps, flagged rather than hidden

  • Only utilities with all four inputs get a rank. Unranked utilities still appear (tick "Include utilities missing an input") with a partial score and a note saying what's missing.
  • Non-IEEE reporters aren't scored on outages. Some large utilities, including Hawaiian Electric, Alabama Power, Oncor and Con Edison, report reliability only under their own methods.
  • Territories overlap. Many counties are served by several utilities, and every one of them gets the county's full storm and wildfire numbers. Utilities whose counties average three or more other providers are flagged.
  • Counties are a coarse stand-in. A utility serving one corner of a large county inherits the whole county's weather and wildfire numbers.

Known limits

  • Storm exposure counts frequency, not strength. A hurricane is one NOAA record per forecast zone, while a stormy summer can add dozens of thunderstorm-wind reports. Severity shows up mainly in the outage-minutes input.
  • Storm reports depend on people noticing. NOAA events are logged by the National Weather Service, partly from spotter and public reports, so populated areas can be over-represented.
  • Forecast zones were translated to counties. Many events are logged by forecast zone; each zone event counts once in every county the zone touches, using the zone map in effect at the time. 0.27% of events used retired zone codes that couldn't be placed and are left out.
  • Wildfire values are national rankings, not raw probabilities. Much of the Southeast ranks high for wildfire likelihood (frequent, often smaller fires), which narrows the gap with the West.
  • Geography quirks: Connecticut uses its 8 pre-2022 counties (as EIA and NOAA do) with one statewide wildfire average. Alaska's Chugach and Copper River areas are shown on the map as the former Valdez-Cordova area.

Sources

  • U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-861, final data 2021–2025.
  • NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Storm Events Database, 2016–2025.
  • National Weather Service, zone–county correlation files, 2019–2026.
  • USDA Forest Service, Wildfire Risk to Communities, county data updated April 2026.
  • U.S. Census Bureau 2020 Gazetteer (land area); county shapes from Census 2017 cartographic boundaries via the us-atlas project.

Every number traces back to a downloaded source file, and the whole page rebuilds from raw data with one command (python build.py). Every judgment call is logged in DECISIONS.md.

Built from public data. Data years: storms 2016–2025, reliability 2021–2025, utility data 2025.
